title: Life cycle energy and environmental assessment (LCEEA)
body: The life cycle impacts of built infrastructure stem from two domains: (a) embodied energy and emissions associated with material production and with construction‐related processes (transportation, site activities, administration), as well as facility management activities (maintenance, repair, replacement/refurbishment) and end-of-life operations (demolition and waste handling); and (b) operational energy use during the use phase. Quantification of embodied impacts is methodologically more complex than that of operational energy because it spans multi-tier supply chains, heterogeneous data sources, and recurrent interventions over the service life.

The LCEEA research addresses this complexity through four research thrusts: (1) development of macroeconomic, input–output–based hybrid life-cycle models to estimate embodied energy and carbon intensities of construction materials and services; (2) comparative assessment of envelope and material alternatives over 50-100-year service lives at the whole-building scale; (3) measurement and modeling of recurrent embodied impacts during facilities management, including the timing and magnitude of repair/replacement events; and (4) implementation of software plug-ins that integrate macroeconomic embodied intensity factors within design and construction environments (e.g., BIM/LCA toolchains) to support early-stage decision-making.

The aim is to operationalize LCEEA metrics as primary criteria for design and procurement in the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) sector. Methodologically, continuing from the 2002 Benchmark Input–Output tables, we construct hybrid econometric models that integrate environmentally extended IO coefficients with statistical datasets (industry production, trade, and price indices). These models yield material- and sector-specific embodied energy and carbon intensities consistent with building system boundaries (A1-A5, B-stage recurrent activities, and C-stage processes) and are applied to bills of quantities and maintenance schedules to produce scenario-robust life-cycle inventories and impact estimates. The resulting datasets, methods, and integration tools have been adopted in multiple federally funded and university-sponsored studies, providing a reproducible basis for life-cycle-consistent evaluation of design, construction, and asset-management choices.
funding: National Science Foundation; Texas A&M University (TAMU); TAMU ASCEND
team: Varusha Venkatraj, Omid Haghighi, Shashank Singh, Pranav Pradeep Kumar, Farshid Mousavi

title: Nexus-centered prognostic multi-objective optimization
body: Buildings impose environmental burdens through both operational energy (OE) during use phase and embodied flows embedded in materials and processes (e.g., manufacturing, construction, transport, maintenance, repair/replacement, and end-of-life). These flows draw on primary and secondary energy and freshwater directly (site activities) and indirectly (material and energy supply chains). A carbon-centered optimization process can therefore shift burdens and unintentionally increase freshwater consumption. In view of accelerating freshwater scarcity, optimization must address the energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus, not just carbon in isolation.

In this research we propose a prognostic, rather than diagnostic, optimization framework that explicitly anticipates non-stationary boundary conditions (climate and energy systems). The framework jointly optimizes embodied energy (EE), operational energy, life-cycle carbon, and embodied water subject to performance and feasibility constraints. We employ metaheuristics (e.g., NSGA-II) on envelope decision variables (e.g., insulation, glazing, window-to-wall ratio, orientation, assembly configurations), evaluating candidates and selecting the optimal solution with current and projected weather (morphed from climate scenarios), and with evolving energy-economy parameters (end-use intensities, electricity generation mix, and usage patterns). This prognostic stance examines design robustness to future climate and grid trajectories.

The research program conducts multi-tier optimization of real-world commercial buildings across all United States sub-climate zones to: (1) quantify EE-OE interdependencies by measuring an EE factor that represents the EE expense of saving one unit of OE; (2) re-evaluate energy-focused design decisions from an ECW nexus lens; and (3) investigate how fast-changing energy mix and use and climate variability may influence future EE-OE interdependencies. Education and dissemination objectives are aligned with the research aims. We integrate physics-based energy modeling and virtual-reality (VR)-enabled learning into curricula and research training to: (a) establish a diagnostic-to-prognostic pedagogy at the university level, (b) strengthen environmental sustainability education in high schools, and (c) translate tools and guidance to architects, engineers, and home builders, enabling broader, societally relevant adoption of ECW-consistent design practice.

title: Forward and Inverse Predictive Analytics for Multi-objective Optimization
body: Forward (surrogate) prediction. Multi-objective optimization (MOO) in early-stage building design is computationally intensive because a high-dimensional decision space must be exhaustively sampled and evaluated, often via many thousands of physics-based simulations. This creates substantial demands for high-performance computing and time. Surrogate modeling offers a tractable alternative by learning an explicit, low-latency approximation of the input–output mapping. In this project, we train forward neural network emulators on Pareto-optimal archives compiled from dozens of real-world commercial buildings. The forward model predicts objective vectors (e.g., energy use, life-cycle carbon, thermal discomfort, cost) from candidate design variables (e.g., WWR, glazing, insulation, orientation) and estimates Pareto-set proximity. This amortizes the cost of optimization: once trained, the emulator enables rapid screening and ranking of designs, markedly reducing the number of expensive simulator calls needed for final verification. Uncertainty quantification (e.g., Monte-Carlo dropout or ensembles) flags low-confidence regions, guiding targeted infill simulations and maintaining accuracy.

Inverse (goal-conditioned) prediction. Conventional MOO frequently operates as a black box, returning non-explanatory “optimal” solutions that may conflict with site constraints or design intent, and that do little to advance design understanding. To address this, we develop an inverse optimization–centered predictive analytics framework that conditions directly on target performance (e.g., limits on life-cycle carbon and adaptive comfort exceedance) and returns feasible design vectors consistent with contextual constraints (climate, code, constructability, hygrothermal risk) and architectural intent. Practically, this is implemented via conditional neural mappings (e.g., conditional density estimators or normalizing flows) that infer distributions over design variables given goals and constraints, yielding sets of admissible, site-specific options rather than a single point solution. Post-hoc explainability (feature attributions, partial-dependence profiles) and constraint diagnostics expose the factors driving recommendations, reducing opacity and enabling science-informed trade-offs between embodied and operational impacts. Together, the forward emulator (for fast evaluation) and the inverse, goal-conditioned predictor (for design synthesis under constraints) provide a scalable pathway to compute-efficient, interpretable multi-objective decision support for low-energy, low-carbon building design.
team: Varusha Venkatraj, Maryam Abbasi Kamazani, Sejal Shanbhag,

title: Life Cycle Assessment of Bio-Based Alternatives for Large-Scale 3D Printing
body: Hempcrete. A substantial proportion of embodied carbon emissions in the building sector arises from the production and use of construction materials, as most rely heavily on fossil fuel–based energy sources. Material selection also significantly affects operational energy use; therefore, reducing both embodied and operational carbon emissions necessitates the development of materials with near-zero or negative embodied carbon and superior thermal performance. This need is particularly pressing given that Portland cement, the dominant material used in extrusion-based 3D printing, accounts for approximately 7% of global carbon emissions.

In this collaborative research, the material design and testing team has developed a novel extrusion-compatible hempcrete mixture for large-scale 3D printing applications. A cradle-to-grave Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) framework was established to evaluate the environmental performance of hempcrete using a hybrid LCA approach that integrates process-based and input–output-based methodologies. The analysis further incorporates projected material requirements due to extreme weather events and geological hazards over an extended building lifespan, thereby ensuring a comprehensive understanding of the material’s long-term environmental implications.

Clay. Supported by the Texas A&M University President’s Excellence Fund (X Grant Program), this project focuses on developing 3D-printable clay composites with multifunctional and adaptive properties. The goal is to produce a sustainable material system capable of being reprocessed and reprinted, promoting circularity within the construction lifecycle. The research team successfully formulated and 3D printed clay mixes at the laboratory scale, followed by a holistic LCA quantifying environmental impacts per unit of mechanical performance. This work advances the understanding of bio-based, reconfigurable materials for additive manufacturing in the built environment.
funding: United States Department of Energy, Advanced Research Projects Agency – Energy (ARPA-E)
team: Yasaman Norouzi, Sejal Shanbhag, Lena Abu Ennab

title: Impact of Climate Change-Induced Extreme Hygrothermal Swings on Building Envelope Performance
body: This collaborative project between Texas A&M University and Pennsylvania State University investigates how climate change-driven variations in temperature and humidity affect the long-term environmental performance of building envelopes. The research examines both embodied and operational carbon impacts over building life cycles exceeding 100 years.

The Penn State team is conducting accelerated weathering tests on representative envelope assemblies to evaluate degradation in thermal resistance, moisture control, and mechanical integrity. The Texas A&M team utilizes this empirical data to model the influence of material deterioration on durability, service life, and energy performance, quantifying the resulting increases in embodied and operational carbon emissions. The analysis integrates future climate projections from CMIP6 models and downscaled datasets from CORDEX, enabling the assessment of dynamic, extreme condition-based life cycle carbon impacts. Future energy grid composition, energy mix evolution, and energy use intensity trends are incorporated to ensure that the embodied carbon estimates reflect projected energy-economic scenarios. The main research goal is to understand how extreme hygrothermal swings may adversely affect building envelope performance in current and future scenarios with hotter and drier decades ahead.

title: Climate Resilience and Environmental Sustainability Nexus
body: Climate change has already begun to manifest through escalating extreme weather events, with the building sector contributing both to its causes and consequences. Accounting for nearly 48% of global annual energy consumption and over 40% of global carbon emissions, the built environment remains a central target for decarbonization. While existing strategies primarily address the mitigation of emissions, the causal dimension of climate change, there is a critical need to also enhance resilience to its consequences. This research introduces a two-pronged nexus-based framework linking environmental sustainability and climate resilience.

Prong 1: The analytical framework connects carbon emissions with durability and service life assessments of materials and assemblies. This approach enables integrated early-stage design decision-making, where material selection is guided by both life cycle carbon intensity and resilience-oriented performance attributes.

Prong 2: A Living Lab methodology is employed to operationalize co-design and community participation in developing and implementing resilience solutions. The City of Port Arthur, Texas, serves as the primary Living Lab, where affected communities, local stakeholders, and research teams co-identify vulnerabilities and co-develop adaptive strategies.

The participatory co-design model ensures that proposed interventions are socially acceptable, contextually relevant, and economically feasible, considering local supply chain and cost constraints. The initiative further engages community organizations, local businesses, and volunteer groups involved in disaster preparedness, response, and recovery, integrating their experiential knowledge into resilience planning.

This multinational collaboration, involving researchers from the United States, Canada, Norway, the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Indonesia, and Colombia, draws expertise from architecture, psychology, materials science, construction science and engineering, social and behavioral sciences, and community development. Beyond Port Arthur, the research includes two additional Living Labs in Medellín, Colombia, and Indramayu, Indonesia, addressing broader resilience domains such as housing, agriculture, fisheries, and watershed management. Collectively, this two-pronged framework advances the science of sustainable and resilient design decision-making while fostering inclusive and durable climate adaptation strategies for vulnerable communities.
funding: New Frontiers in Research Fund, Canada Research Coordinating Committee

title: Serious Games for Environmental Awareness and Construction Training
body: BIMThermoVR. Our team is developing a gamified, immersive Virtual Reality (VR) platform to improve high school students’ understanding of the building sector’s energy and environmental impacts. Within a virtual single-family house, learners navigate the environment and adjust design parameters such as, window-to-wall ratio, orientation, and insulation levels to observe how these changes affect embodied and operational energy outcomes. We employ BIMThermoVR to deliver engaging, interactive activities and evaluate changes in environmental awareness using pre- and post-instruction surveys.

Virtual Construction Lab (VCL). VCL is a gamified VR interface that provides experiential training in the virtual construction of wall sections using digital materials and support systems. The primary objective is to simulate construction workflows across Levels of Development (LOD): users begin with a simplified “Lego-block” wall, progress to a more detailed assembly with concrete blocks and reinforcement, and ultimately employ support tools (e.g., a virtual ladder) to complete a detailed wall build.
funding: New Frontiers in Research Fund, Canada Research Coordinating Committee
